strengths: Novel and well-articulated problem formulation distinguishing intrinsic hallucination from hallucination propagation in multi-agent VLM systems
Comprehensive and convincing empirical analysis with turn-wise, layer-wise, and token-wise attention studies across 6 VLMs demonstrating 62% attention reduction in middle layers
Consistent improvements across diverse settings: 8 benchmarks, 4 MAS structures, 10 base models (2.4-4.4% average gains, stronger on challenging benchmarks)
Practical, plug-and-play method design with minimal overhead and compatibility with modern acceleration techniques (Flash-Attention support via Key-Norm alternative)
Well-designed ablation studies with five distinct token subset categories (random, inactive, rise, fall, unimodal) validating the approach
Novel hallucination snowballing (HS) metric capturing both severity and propagation distance that benefits the broader community
Thorough appendix with hyperparameter sensitivity analysis and comprehensive experimental settings supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (temperature scaling, attention-based token selection, masking) are standard techniques; core contribution is problem identification rather than novel mechanisms

Unclear theoretical justification for why visual relay tokens prevent propagation; Equation 1 contextualizes visual tokens with instructions, potentially reintroducing the text-bias problem the method aims to solve
Insufficient explanation of why existing single-agent hallucination methods (MemVR, VISTA, DeCo, TAME) perform worse than baseline in multi-agent settings, raising fairness concerns about comparisons
Modest individual component contributions (Table 6: 0.2-2.0% impact); unclear whether gains come from specific mechanism design or simply additional visual information
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to visual QA tasks; other hallucination types (spatial, attribute, relational) unexplored; single-turn scenarios show minimal improvement (Figure 7)
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, significance tests, or multiple seeds reported; some improvements are modest (0.5-1.5% on MME/MMBench)
Key-Norm approximation shows degradation vs. attention scores (Table 7) and uses ad-hoc 3×3 buffer; only ~70% overlap with original selection raises approximation quality concerns
Generalization limitations: restricted to 7B-34B models, truncated analysis at 20 turns, only tested on distributed MAS architectures, parameters tuned on circular structure
